1:
The opening clause is one of the old difficulties, and each voice meets it differently. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says the only possible literal rendering is that Saul was the son of one year when he began to reign, that the corruption or gap in the text dates from a far back period, and that the English version is simply a probable but conjectural paraphrase; he notes that the Chaldee and some Rabbis interpret it of Saul as an innocent child. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) argue from the form of words instead: by the standing custom in the history of the kings such a notice opens with the king’s age at his accession and the length of his reign, and comparison with the accession formulas of Ishbosheth and David and the kings of Judah leaves no doubt that this verse was meant to do the same, so that a number has dropped out. John Gill (reformed) collects three readings: that Saul had a son a year old when he began to reign, namely Ishbosheth, who was forty when his father died; that there is an ellipsis of the number; or that the words are figurative, of one like a child for purity and innocence.

The three thousand men are read as a turning point in the nation’s story. Ellicott calls it a very important statement, telling us of the first beginning of a standing army in Israel and the first step towards her development into a great military power; it was Saul’s military genius and foresight, he judges, that enabled David and Solomon to make the conquests which raised Israel for a time among the greatest of Eastern powers, while Saul’s own great life was frittered away repelling domestic enemies. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the same number tactically, that Saul divided his men and sent them against the garrisons at Michmash and Bethel and Gibeah, hoping by surprising them to get swords and spears for his people, of which the chapter later says they were entirely destitute. Gill supplies the arithmetic, that the three thousand were drawn from the three hundred thousand who had gone against the Ammonites, some as a guard about Saul’s person and the rest a standing force.

At the muster of the Philistines the numbers are challenged three ways. Clarke finds no proportion between the chariots and the cavalry, observing that the largest armies ever brought into the field, even by mighty emperors, were never furnished with thirty thousand chariots, and judges the word for thirty a false reading for three, the Syriac and the Arabic both giving three thousand. Ellicott calls the figures perfectly untrustworthy and argues from the rolls of ancient armies, in which the war chariots are always fewer than the horsemen, whereas here they are made four times as numerous. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keeps the figure and changes the word, supposing most of them carriages for baggage rather than chariots of war.

On the flight into the caves the comment is practical. Clarke explains it by numbers and equipment, that the Israelites were few and totally unarmed as to swords and spears and were terrified at so numerous and well-appointed an army, Judea being full of rocks and caves where men might shelter; some hid, others fled beyond Jordan, and those who clave to Saul followed him trembling. Gill reports that Abarbinel refers the clause about the people being distressed not to Israel at all but to the other side. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets the whole retreat under a judgment: we are not told wherein Israel had offended so as to forfeit God’s presence and turn his hand against them, but doubtless they had left God, else he would not have left them — and Saul, he adds, was weak and impolitic and did not order his affairs with discretion.
8:
Which appointment the set time refers to is a real chronological problem. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) cuts it by denying the obvious reference: what is said here cannot be understood of the order given when Saul was anointed but of a different appointment, Samuel having promised on this occasion to come within seven days and having kept his word, since he arrived before the day was out. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) feels the difficulty of referring back to the day of Saul’s prophetic consecration, which took place at least three or four years and perhaps much longer before this, especially as the two men had certainly been together at Gilgal in the meantime; yet the extraordinary solemnity of that earlier warning draws him back towards it. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) offers two harmonisations, that the order though recorded earlier may have been given afterwards, or that it was given as a general rule to be observed at every public gathering at Gilgal. On the day itself John Gill (reformed) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agree that Saul tarried to the seventh day but not to the end of it, the last day not being finished.

What the sin actually was divides them three against one. Clarke holds the act itself unlawful, calling it most perfectly unconstitutional, since Saul had no authority to offer, or even to cause to be offered, any of the Lord’s sacrifices. Ellicott denies that this is the charge at all: many have supposed the greatness of Saul’s sin lay in offering with his own hand, but not a hint of it is anywhere given us, and it is more than probable that the sacrifice, offered so prematurely in the absence of the seer, was performed by the hand of the priest who was no doubt in attendance on the king — so that there was no unlawful assumption of priestly functions. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the Hebrew the same way, that the phrase does not imply Saul offered with his own hand or performed the priestly function on this occasion. Gill settles it from the rebuke itself: Saul is charged with not waiting the full time, and with intruding into the priest’s office he is not charged.

Saul’s defence is itemised and then weighed. Clarke counts three excuses — that the people were fast leaving his standard, that Samuel had not come at the very commencement of the time though he came within it, and that the Philistines were coming fast upon him — and judges that in all this Saul was sincere but rash, and regardless of a precept he had evidently received. Ellicott puts the king’s position more bluntly still, that he would gratefully receive any help the prophet could bring but in such an emergency preferred, sooner than run any risk, to act alone and if necessary to go into battle without divine consecration. Keil and Delitzsch supply the fear behind it, that Saul acted in anxiety lest the people lose heart and forsake him altogether if there were further delay. Wesley glosses the admission that he forced himself as meaning against his own mind and inclination.

The sentence is read narrowly rather than broadly. Gill takes the kingdom that shall not continue to mean not in Saul’s family nor in his tribe, but removed to another. Wesley qualifies what was forfeited, observing that the phrase for ever in scripture often signifies only a long time, so that it would have been abundantly verified had the kingdom been enjoyed by Saul and by his son and by his son’s son, after whom it might have come to Judah in any case. Gill notices the timing, that Samuel arrived after the burnt offering was ended but before the peace offerings could be offered.
15:
What Samuel’s going up to Gibeah signified is read four ways, and the voices do not even agree whether the two men travelled together. John Gill (reformed) sees anger in the manner of it, that Samuel arose seemingly in wrath and displeasure and did not stay to offer the peace offerings which remained, though he thinks Saul followed him or at least came after. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads the departure as abandonment with a reservation: Saul has set up for himself and is now left to himself, and it does not appear that Samuel either prayed with him or directed him; yet by going to Saul’s own city he intimated that he had not quite abandoned him but waited to do him a kindness another time — or else, Henry allows, he went to the college of the prophets there, to pray for Saul when he did not think fit to pray with him. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) has them go together and makes the journey an act of support, since David though appointed in the divine purpose is not to displace Saul during his life, so that Samuel accompanies him to give the requisite help in this conjuncture. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) has Samuel pass from Gilgal alone, but judges that he does not yet break off friendly relations, and wonders whether the noble old man still hoped the brilliant and gallant king would recognise his fatal error.

Ellicott also charges the English translators with an outright mistake here, and diagnoses its cause. Saul and Jonathan, uniting their sadly diminished forces, entrench themselves at Geba, in a strong position at the end of a pass from which they could watch the Philistines, their small number forbidding any thought of attack; and where the version reads Gibeah of Benjamin it should read Geba of Benjamin, the translators having probably been led astray by the mention of Gibeah in the verse before.

The size of what was left is stated without comment and lands hard. Clarke notes that the six hundred were the whole of the Israelitish army at this time, and not one sword or spear among them. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) treat what follows as continuous with this, holding that the account of Israel’s disarming belongs with the foregoing so far as the facts are concerned, since it was Jonathan’s brave deed and the splendid victory it brought that terminated the war for which Saul had sought help.

That the raiders could go out in three companies at all is itself the point. Gill turns it into a reproach: Saul did not dare come out to fight, and there was none in the land to oppose them, so the Philistines sent three companies to ravage the country — of so little use and service was a king to Israel, which they had been so extremely desirous of, and this was suffered to convince them of their vain confidence. Clarke reads the division tactically and looks ahead, that the Philistines finding the Israelites durst not risk a battle split their army in three to pillage, and that Jonathan profited by the circumstance and attacked what remained at Michmash. Ellicott cautions that the compiler does not profess to give a detailed account of this or any of Saul’s wars, and supposes the great armed demonstration had completely cowed the Israelites, at least in the south. Gill fixes one of the three roads, that Beth-horon named two cities, the upper and the nether, both in Ephraim, lying northwest of the Philistine camp at Michmash and some eight miles from it.
19:
How Israel came to have no smith at all is explained from policy and from parallel. John Gill (reformed) says the Philistines, while they ruled, had removed the smiths into their own country and forbidden any to learn or exercise the trade in Israel. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) thinks it likely they were carried off in the former wars, and sets two parallels beside it: Porsenna, in the peace he granted the Romans, permitted no iron to be forged except for the purposes of agriculture, and the Chaldeans did the same to the Jews in the time of Nebuchadnezzar, carrying away all the artificers. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) limits the claim instead, allowing a year or perhaps two or three to have elapsed while Saul and Jonathan abode in Gibeah and the raids went on unchecked, and judging that the statement about the destruction of the smithies probably refers specially to the southern districts of Canaan.

Ellicott reaches the same Roman parallel, that Porsenna allowed the Romans iron implements for agriculture only; Clarke presses it further to mark a difference, finding from this passage that the Philistines did not grant Israel even as much as Porsenna granted Rome, since he at least permitted the people to manufacture the implements of husbandry. On where they had to go the two part company. Gill has them obliged to go into Philistia, to one or other of the cities or garrisons where the trade was exercised. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) denies it was the land of the Philistines at all, but the stations and garrisons they retained within Israel’s own territory, Samuel’s authority having so far overawed them that they durst not give much disturbance; in these, he says, the Philistines kept all the smiths. Of the implements themselves Ellicott admits defeat, noting that the word rendered coulter is elsewhere given as ploughshare by most of the older versions, and that we cannot now distinguish the two with any precision.

The next verse is the chapter’s other old crux. Clarke reports that the Hebrew noun, from a root meaning to rub hard, is translated very differently by the versions and by critics, and settles for the received sense as likely as any, that the people were allowed the use of files — though he suspects the word means a grindstone — to restore the blunted edges of their tridents and axes and goads. Ellicott grants that this rendering is supported by the Targum and by many of the great Hebrew commentators, Rashi among them, but reports that Gesenius and the majority of modern scholars render the word instead by bluntness, so that the passage would say there was dulness of edge upon the mattocks and the rest. Gill offers a third arrangement, that the words may be joined to the verse before, so that it was to the Philistines they went to sharpen the tools when their edges were blunt.

That no sword or spear was found raises an objection, and two answers are given to it. Clarke states the difficulty squarely: if Israel enjoyed such profound peace and undisturbed dominion under Samuel, how were they totally destitute of arms, a state which argues the lowest circumstances of oppression and vassalage? His answer is to distinguish the weapons, since the bow and the sling were the principal arms of Israel and for these they needed no smith at all. Ellicott answers by narrowing the scope, that the words must not be pressed too literally and that the absence of arms held in the open valleys of southern Canaan, especially the Benjamite territory, which were just the districts from which Saul and Jonathan could most easily have recruited their thinned and dispirited forces. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep to the inventory, giving the share and coulter, the axe and mattock, and the goads that were sharpened.
